questions.explanation: The test is entirely about whether anyone is left worse off, so a change that helps at least one person and harms nobody satisfies it by definition. A Kaldor-Hicks test asks only whether the gainers could in principle compensate the losers, which a change that actually harms someone can pass, so the two conditions are not interchangeable. A rise in total utility says nothing about the loser, and a Nash equilibrium describes incentives rather than anyone's welfare.

questions.explanation: The utilitarian rule aggregates by summation, so an outcome is better whenever its total utility is larger, which is what lets it trade a large gain to one person against a small loss to another. questions.explanation: A deadweight loss is the difference between total surplus at the efficient quantity and total surplus at the distorted one, so it captures the gains from trade that no longer happen. Revenue and any surplus that merely shifts from buyers to producers are transfers, and since total surplus is unchanged by a transfer they contribute nothing to the loss. What disappears under a distortion is the set of mutually beneficial trades that are never made, and the size of the missing triangle between demand and supply measures exactly that.

questions.explanation: A public good is defined by non-rivalrous consumption, so one person's use leaves the same amount available to everybody else, and by inexcludability, so a non-payer cannot be kept out without also denying it to payers. Rivalrousness and excludability together are the properties of an ordinary private good, and mixing one property from each category describes nothing in particular. It is the pair that matters, since a good that is non-rivalrous but easily excludable, such as a subscription broadcast, is instead a club good.

questions.explanation: A common-pool resource is non-excludable but rivalrous, and because each user sees only its own effect on the stock, each extracts more than the socially efficient amount, so total effort exceeds the efficient level and the stock is stripped faster. Each would extract less if it internalised the harm its own effort does to everyone else's catch, so the efficient outcome requires a smaller total effort than the one chosen. The resource is not conserved, since nobody has an incentive to conserve it, and the harm arrives gradually through lower catches rather than in a single instant.

questions.stem: Every unit produced here imposes 6 dollars of external damage with marginal cost of 20 dollars a unit and demand of 60 dollars minus quantity. Explain how a tax set at 6 dollars a unit moves the market to the efficient outcome.
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why a corrective tax restores efficiency

answer.exemplar: A strong answer notes that the benefit of the good is the same for both people whoever pays, so once one person has paid the other enjoys the full 16 dollars for nothing. Each therefore compares a 10 dollar cost with the 16 dollars it would receive and concludes that someone else should pay, and since both conclude the same, voluntary provision is zero and the 22 dollars of available surplus is never created. The wrong version says the good is not worth providing, which the 16 dollars against 10 dollars figure refutes directly. A second wrong version proposes a rule that makes each provide, but any such rule needs somebody to enforce it, which is a cost the voluntary scheme has not accounted for.

questions.explanation: The benefit of the good is identical for both people whoever pays for it, so once one person has contributed the other collects the full 16 dollars at no cost of its own. Each therefore treats a 10 dollar contribution as avoidable, and since both reach that conclusion together, voluntary provision falls to zero and the 22 dollars of available surplus is never created. The good is plainly worth more than it costs, so the difficulty is not valuation but the fact that one person's payment buys a benefit the other receives for nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what each person gets by contributing nothing at all.
questions.learningObjective: explain the free-rider logic behind public underprovision

questions.stem: Each of two people values a public good at 16 dollars and would pay 10 dollars to provide it, so one person providing alone yields 22 dollars of surplus. Explain why private contributions typically fail to secure that good.
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why free riding underprovides a public good

answer.exemplar: A strong answer distinguishes two effects. Some of the surplus that sellers used to receive is now paid by buyers at a lower price, so part of the buyers' gain is a transfer from sellers rather than new gain. At the same time only 8 of the 15 units that would have been traded are traded, and the 7 units in between were worth more to buyers than they cost to make, so 49 dollars of genuine surplus disappears. The wrong version says the ceiling only redistributes and destroys nothing, which ignores the untraded units entirely. A second wrong version claims buyers as a group gain, forgetting that their gain is smaller than the sellers' loss plus the lost trades.

questions.explanation: Two effects run side by side. The lower price moves part of the sellers' surplus to buyers, and because a transfer leaves total surplus unchanged it is not a cost to the economy. Separately, only 8 of the 15 units that would have been traded are traded, and the 7 units in between were worth more to buyers than they cost to make, so 49 dollars of genuine surplus is destroyed. Counting only the transfer produces the claim that a ceiling merely redistributes, and counting only the deadweight loss misses the transfer that makes ceilings attractive politically.
questions.hint: Separate the trades that still happen from the trades that stop.
questions.learningObjective: explain what a binding price ceiling does to surplus

questions.stem: Demand is 40 dollars minus quantity, supply is 10 dollars plus quantity, and a binding ceiling of 18 dollars holds the price below its 25 dollar equilibrium. Explain what happens to total surplus and to its distribution.
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS

answer.exemplar: A strong answer starts from the first-best position: with no other distortion, a tax equal to the marginal external cost would push output to the efficient level exactly. Once another distortion is present, the output that a tax of that size produces is no longer the efficient output, because the untaxed distortion has already moved the market away from it, so the best available tax is a compromise whose size trades the externality's remaining harm against the extra harm it does elsewhere. That is what makes the problem second best: there is no policy that is right, only the least damaging one. The wrong version simply reuses the first-best tax and calls the result optimal, which fixes the externality while leaving the second distortion to push output in the opposite direction.

questions.explanation: With no other distortion present, a tax equal to the marginal external cost lands output exactly on the efficient quantity, and that is the first-best calibration. Once a second distortion has already shifted output away from that point, the same tax drives quantity past the efficient level, so the best available rate is a smaller compromise trading the externality's remaining harm against extra harm inflicted elsewhere. Reusing the first-best rate and calling the result optimal leaves the second distortion uncorrected while over-correcting the first.
questions.hint: Ask what the ideal policy would be if the other distortion were absent.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a second-best policy must match its distortion

questions.explanation: The 8 units sold are worth 288 dollars in total, and at 18 dollars they cost 144, so consumer surplus is 144. Total surplus is 225 dollars at the efficient 15 units and 176 at the 8 units a ceiling allows, so the deadweight loss is 49. The 32 dollar figure in the third option is producer surplus, and 176 is total surplus after the ceiling rather than the amount lost, so it is smaller than the efficient total instead of being the difference.
questions.hint: Take the area under demand down to 8 units, then compare total surplus at 8 and 15 units.

questions.explanation: Social marginal cost is 20 dollars of private cost plus 6 dollars of damage, and 60 minus q equal to 26 gives an efficient output of 34 units. A tax of exactly 6 dollars a unit makes the producer face that 26 dollar figure and land on the same 34 units, so the second stage is just the first one reversed. Output of 40 units is the unregulated private choice and the starting point, and taxing 20 dollars would drive output below 34, over-correcting a distortion of 6 dollars.
questions.hint: Meet the demand curve with marginal cost plus the external damage, then read off the tax.

questions.explanation: Thirty percent of 168 dollars is 50.40 dollars of resources consumed by lobbying, and the 168 dollars of revenue minus that waste and the 36 dollar deadweight loss of the tax leaves 81.60 dollars. Omitting the tax's own distortion overstates the gain by 36 dollars, which is the 117.60 dollar figure in the second option, so a policy can look nearly costless once the rent-seeking is counted but not once the distortion is. The waste is a genuine loss because it buys no output, whereas the revenue itself is only a transfer.
questions.hint: Take the stated share of revenue, then subtract both the waste and the distortion loss.

questions.explanation: The utilitarian rule compares totals of 40 dollars in state A and 50 dollars in state B, so it selects B and the first stage answer is 50. The worst-off person enjoys 20 dollars in A and 0 in B, so choosing B costs that person 20 dollars of utility. A maximin rule would have chosen A for exactly that reason, and the gap between the two criteria is a disagreement about whether a large gain to one person can offset eliminating the other, not an arithmetic difference.
questions.hint: Compare the sums, then compare the minimum utility across the two states.
questions.learningObjective: compare two social welfare criteria and the cost of the choice
